challenges.name: supply-chain-attack-surface-quiz
challenges.title: Where does someone else's code get in?
challenges.description: Two pieces of evidence from the CodeDev build pipeline: a provenance attestation for a dependency release, and the same GitHub Actions step running different code on two days.

questions.question:
The content-tools build depends on @fastgrade/runner. After installing 4.2.1:

$ npm audit signatures
audited 419 packages in 2s
419 packages have verified registry signatures
37 packages have verified attestations

The attestation of @fastgrade/runner@4.2.1 says:
  source:   github.com/fastgrade/runner @ commit 9f3c2e1
  workflow: .github/workflows/release.yml (GitHub Actions)

$ git log -1 --format='%h %an %s' 9f3c2e1   (in the fastgrade/runner repository)
9f3c2e1 maint-bot chore: bump deps

The commit was pushed directly to main; no pull request references it.

Statement: "The verified attestation shows that 4.2.1 contains only code that was reviewed in the fastgrade/runner repository."
questions.explanation: False. Provenance links the tarball to a repository, a commit and a workflow, and the signature proves that link was not forged after the build. It says nothing about whether the commit was reviewed or written by the maintainers: here commit 9f3c2e1 was pushed straight to main, which is exactly what an attacker with a stolen maintainer token can do, and the release workflow would sign the result just the same. What the attestation does give you is where to look: the commit and the workflow run. The misconception is that "verified" means "safe"; it means "built where it says it was built".

questions.question:
Workflow of the CodeDev web app (unchanged since September):

jobs:
  build:
    permissions: write-all
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: cachekit/setup-cache@v3
      - run: npm ci --ignore-scripts

Actions log, Monday run 18790:
  Download action repository 'cachekit/setup-cache@v3' (SHA:4b1e0c7a92f5d3e8a1c6b0f2d9e47a3c5b8f1d20)
Actions log, Thursday run 18902:
  Download action repository 'cachekit/setup-cache@v3' (SHA:e93d51f08a2c7b4e6f1d0a9c3b85e2f7d4a6c019)

The cachekit/setup-cache repository shows no new release between Monday and Thursday.

Statement: "The code that ran as cachekit/setup-cache@v3 changed between Monday and Thursday although the workflow file did not, and pinning the step to the full commit SHA from Monday would have kept Monday's code."
questions.explanation: True. A tag such as v3 is a movable pointer in someone else's repository: the log shows it resolved to two different commits, and with no release in between, someone moved it. A full-length commit SHA is immutable, so `uses: cachekit/setup-cache@4b1e0c7a92f5d3e8a1c6b0f2d9e47a3c5b8f1d20` runs the same code until you change the line in a reviewed pull request. With `permissions: write-all`, the changed action could also push to the repository or create a release with the job's token, which is why lesson 9 narrows permissions per job. The misconception is that a version-looking tag is as fixed as a version number on the registry.
